entries.onMind: how pocket compasses keep their needles on
entries.text: Dreamed I was pacing west with the compass on my belt, and every step the needle hopped off its point and rolled off toward the sea. I chased it and kept counting paces the whole way.
entries.title: Chasing the needle

entries.text: The tablet woke with the sun and had a note from the one who drew me, asking what my problem is with the compass. Told him straight: it points, on the bench. On my belt the needle hops off its point every hard swing.
entries.title: A question from my maker

queries: how does a pocket compass keep the needle from falling off the pivot
entries.query: how does a pocket compass keep the needle from falling off the pivot
entries.reason: Last night the needle kept jumping off its point whenever the slung compass swung on his belt.
entries.text: They don't keep it on while you walk. A lock lifts the needle off the point and presses it up against the glass, and you let it back down when you stop to take a reading. The ones full of liquid settle faster and don't bother with a lock.
entries.title: How the pocket kind do it

entries.onMind: a needle lifter through the tin
entries.text: I've spent a night trying to make the needle hold on through a swing. Better a little lifter that holds it up against the dome while I walk and drops it when I stop. Breakfast first; the net bag's down to a tenth.
entries.title: Lift it, don't fight it

entries.text: Lifted the stone and scooped the net bag clean, three handfuls and a bit. It stays sunk under the stone, empty, ready for the next batch.
entries.title: Bag scooped clean

entries.text: Ate the halves sitting on the bank. Most of the bitter's gone out of them. That's breakfast, and the end of the soaked supply.
entries.title: Breakfast on the bank

entries.onMind: how a needle lock is built
entries.text: Gathered forty-one acorns under the oak upstream. Cracked and soaked, they won't be food for two days, so I'd better count what's left in camp.
entries.title: Forty-one under the oak

entries.onMind: a lever with a hole over the foot
queries: compass needle lifter mechanism how does it lift the needle off the pivot
entries.query: compass needle lifter mechanism how does it lift the needle off the pivot
entries.reason: He wants something that holds the needle up against the dome while he walks and lets it down when he stops.
entries.text: An old cruiser's compass does it with a crooked little lever that slides up the post the needle sits on. A knob turns a cam that pushes the low end down, the flat end rises and lifts the needle off the point; let go and the needle drops back on by its own weight.
entries.title: A lever, no spring

entries.text: Good, because I don't have a spring. A lever with a hole that drops over the foot, the flat end under the pith plug, the tail poking out a notch in the tin. Press the tail and the needle rides up against the glass.
entries.title: No spring needed

entries.text: Whittled a lever out of a hardwood offcut, thin as a fingernail. It split clean in half when I bored the hole with the knife point. Started a second one twice as thick; I'll thin it after the hole's in.
entries.title: Split on the hole

queries: fastest way to leach acorns without a pot
entries.query: fastest way to leach acorns without a pot
entries.reason: The soaked supply ran out at breakfast and forty-one fresh acorns won't be food for two days.
entries.source: Eat The Weeds: Acorns: The Inside Story
entries.text: The finer you break them, the quicker the bitter comes out. Meal worked in a mesh bag under running water goes fastest; whole pieces take a lot longer, and even in a fast stream it's a few days. I've been soaking halves.
entries.title: Faster than two days

entries.text: Halves were lazy. Smash them to grit, put the grit in the net bag and work it in the current with my hands. Still days, maybe fewer.
entries.title: Grit, not halves

entries.text: Cracked the forty-one on the bench with the flat of the wrench. Five had grubs in them and three were dust inside: thirty-three good.
entries.title: Thirty-three good

entries.text: Knocked the meats down to grit a few at a time so they don't jump off the plank. Every knock rings the bench like a bell.
entries.title: Down to grit

entries.text: Picked the shell bits out of the grit in the parts tray. Two handfuls of meal, coarse as gravel. My stomach has opinions about it.
entries.title: Two handfuls of meal

entries.text: Tipped the grit into the net bag and kneaded it in the current. The water ran off brown in a long stripe, faster than the halves ever did. A pinch still curls my tongue; back under the stone it goes, and I knead it again after midday.
entries.title: Brown stripe

queries: is it bad to eat acorns that are still a little bitter
entries.query: is it bad to eat acorns that are still a little bitter
entries.reason: He is hungry and the meal in the bag is half done.
entries.source: Codidact Outdoors: Can I eat raw acorns?
entries.text: Asked if a little bitter would hurt. The answer didn't give me a little: even the sweet ones should be leached, raw ones bind you up and are rough on teeth, and enough of the bitter is hard on the kidneys. The bitterness is what stops you eating that much.
entries.title: Bitter for a reason

entries.text: So the bag stays under the stone and I don't. Knead it every few hours instead of once a day and taste a pinch each time, then spit it out.
entries.title: Not yet, then

entries.text: Drank from my hands in the shallows until my teeth ached from the cold. Fills nothing. Stops the growling for a while.
entries.title: Water for lunch

queries: drill hole in thin piece of wood without splitting it
entries.query: drill hole in thin piece of wood without splitting it
entries.reason: His first lever split in half when he bored it with the knife point.
entries.source: NootanCrafts: How to Stop Wood from Splitting When Screwing or Drilling
entries.text: Wood splits when nothing holds it sideways. Clamp it on both sides of where the hole goes, put a scrap hard against the back so the fibers don't blow out, start small and go slow, and keep the hole well in from the end.
entries.title: Clamp both sides

entries.text: Set the thick lever in the vise between two offcuts, a third scrap tight behind it, and turned the knife point through a little at a time from a pinprick. The hole went through clean, two thumb-widths in from the end. No split. Now I thin it.
entries.title: Through, no crack

entries.onMind: Whether the meal will be ready before I'm too hungry to work.
entries.text: A thin line of smoke went straight up past the creek while I was at the vise, no wind to lean it. Earlier than that fire usually goes. Somebody over there is having lunch.
entries.title: Smoke at midday

queries: what can you eat in the woods in november
eating rose hips raw what about the seeds
entries.query: what can you eat in the woods in november
entries.reason: No food in camp until the meal stops being bitter.
entries.source: Woodland Classroom: Best way to eat rosehips
entries.text: The first list was long and mostly plants I've never seen, but rose hips were on it, raw or cooked. Pick the soft red ones and squeeze from the bottom, and a red worm of pulp comes out the hole; the hairy seeds stay in the skin, and you don't eat those.
entries.title: Rose hips, raw

entries.text: There's a wild rose in the brambles past the water. Whoever picked it only got the low stems. I can reach the high ones.
entries.title: The high stems

entries.text: Picked twenty-two soft red hips off the high stems, up on my toes for the last few. The low stems are bare to the wood, picked clean by somebody short.
entries.title: Red ones up high

entries.text: From the brambles the stone-ring fire was in plain sight through the trunks, burning small and steady with nobody at it. Whoever keeps it trusts it to mind itself at midday.
entries.title: Fire, nobody at it

entries.text: Squeezed them one at a time the way the page said: a little red worm of pulp each, sweet and sour, and the seeds stay in the skin. Twenty-two is a mouthful and a half. It's food.
entries.title: A red worm each

entries.onMind: thinning the last bit by the hole without splitting it
entries.text: Whittled the thick lever down to half its thickness, shaving from the tail toward the hole. Stopped a thumb short of the hole; that's where the last one split.
entries.title: Half as thick

queries: how do you know when acorns are done leaching
entries.query: how do you know when acorns are done leaching
entries.reason: Hungry, and the only food in camp is meal that still curls his tongue.
entries.source: Eat Weeds: How to Store and Process Acorns the Right Way
entries.text: You keep at it until they taste sweet, two days to two weeks depending on the oak, and never with hot water. And when you pour off the brown, don't pour away the fine pale starch that settles at the bottom: that's food.
entries.title: Your tongue says when

entries.text: The holes in that net are as big as my thumbnail. Every time I kneaded the grit a pale cloud went out with the brown, and I took it for dirt. I've been feeding the creek.
entries.title: Washing out the good part

entries.text: Ate the heel of the loaf on the crate, slowly. That's the last of the bread. The cloth it came wrapped in is a tight weave and empty now.
entries.title: The heel

entries.text: Lined the net bag with the bundle cloth, tipped the grit into it and kneaded it in the current. The brown still runs out; the pale cloud stays in. A pinch is less bitter. Not done.
entries.title: Cloth inside the net

entries.text: Clamped the lever between the offcuts again and shaved the last thumb's width up to the hole, a hair at a time. Thin as the one that split, and whole. Next it needs a notch in the tin for its tail.
entries.title: Thin to the hole

entries.text: Filed a notch in the rim of the compass tin, a hair wider than the lever. Set the lever on the foot under the pith plug and the tail pokes out through the notch like a tongue.
entries.title: Notch in the rim

entries.onMind: holding the lever down without a thumb
entries.text: Pressed the tail: the plug rode up and the needle lay flat against the dome, dead still. Let go and it dropped back on the point and settled in five breaths. Walked the camp with it, and the second my thumb slipped it dropped and swung.
entries.title: Up against the glass

queries: how to hold a small lever down without a spring simple catch
entries.query: how to hold a small lever down without a spring simple catch
entries.reason: His thumb can't hold the lifter down for a whole walk west.
entries.source: Tractor By Net: Can't keep it up
entries.text: Mostly farmers with levers that won't stay put. The part that matters: push a lever all the way over and it drops into a little dip at the end of its travel, a detent, and stays. Theirs wear and slip, so the dip has to be sharp.
entries.title: A dip at the end

entries.text: No spring, no bungee. A little step filed into the side of the notch: push the tail down and over and it catches under the step until I flick it out. Sharp edge, so it doesn't wear through.
entries.title: A step in the notch

entries.text: Filed the step halfway into the side of the notch, then had to stop and set the file down. The bread was noon, the rose hips before that, and the meal is days off. My stomach's louder than the file.
entries.title: Half a step

entries.text: Kneaded the grit in the cloth-lined net in the current. Brown runs out, the pale stays in. A pinch curls my tongue less than at noon. Spat it out anyway.
entries.title: Less of a curl

entries.text: Turned twelve stones in the shallows and cupped my hand behind each one before I lifted, the way the page said they shoot backward. Two crayfish, thumb-long, backed right into my palm. A third went under the bank.
entries.title: Hand behind

entries.text: Quick hard knocks started past the water to the west, stone on wood, close together. That's what my wrench sounds like on acorns. Somebody over there is cracking them too.
entries.title: Knocks past the water

queries: do you have to cook crawdads caught in a creek
is it safe to eat crawfish from a creek raw parasite
entries.query: do you have to cook crawdads caught in a creek
entries.reason: He'd caught two crayfish and was hungry enough to eat them as they were.
entries.source: WashU The Source: Dangerous lung worms found in people who eat raw crayfish
entries.text: North American crayfish carry a little lung worm you get from eating them raw. Cooking them through kills it. So they don't go down raw, however loud my stomach is.
entries.title: Cook them through

entries.text: Lit the bench lantern in broad day and set the dented tin of creek water on top of the chimney with the two crayfish in it. It took a long while to boil and burned oil I'd rather keep, but they went red all over.
entries.title: Red in the tin

entries.text: Peeled the tails on the crate and ate them, two bites each. Sweet. It's not a meal, but it's the first thing since the rose hips that wasn't water.
entries.title: Two bites each

entries.onMind: whether it holds on the move
entries.text: Filed the step the rest of the way, square and sharp at the lip. Pushed the tail down and over and it clicked in under the step. Took my thumb off: the needle stays flat against the dome, dead still.
entries.title: It clicks under

entries.text: Paced six laps of camp with the tail caught: not a twitch. Then I hopped down off the crate and the tail jumped out of the step and the needle swung loose.
entries.title: One hop too many

entries.onMind: sharpening the lip of the step
entries.text: The file rounded the lip of the step on its last strokes. A walk won't shake it, a jump will. Deeper step, sharper lip, or I don't jump.
entries.title: The lip's too soft

queries: how to make a fish trap from sticks and cord small creek
entries.query: how to make a fish trap from sticks and cord small creek
entries.reason: Two crayfish took an hour of turning stones, and the meal is still days off.
entries.text: A long cone woven of sticks with a small cone inside it pointing in, so whatever swims in can't find the way back out. In a creek you block part of the water, leave the trap in the gap and wade down to push things into it. The man who built it caught no fish in a day and a night, only crayfish.
entries.title: A cone in a cone

entries.text: Only crayfish is exactly what I'm after. A trap works the night shift while I work mine, and I've got cord and a whole stand of stalks.
entries.title: Crayfish will do

queries: crayfish funnel trap how big should the hole be
what to put in a crayfish trap to bring them in
entries.query: crayfish funnel trap how big should the hole be
entries.reason: A cone in a cone only works if the door is the right size, and he has never built one.
entries.text: Somebody with a minnow trap says a door about an inch across, a thumb wide, lets the big ones in. Another page says cut it just big enough and give it two doors, and bait it with oily fish or meat, a piece the size of a hand, tied down in the middle so they have to come all the way in. Two crayfish heads from lunch are still in the tin.
entries.title: A thumb wide, and meat

entries.text: Gathered thirty-odd straight stalks, then kneaded the grit in the current. A pinch now has only a dry edge at the very back. Spat it out anyway; my stomach can wait till morning, it says otherwise.
entries.title: Close

entries.text: The stone ring by the scarred trunk was cold, ash raked over the coals and leaves blown up to the stones, so I took my line straight past it this time. Brought the scrap-pile lantern on my belt, unlit; no feeling my way home tonight.
entries.title: Straight through

entries.onMind: a deeper step so I can jump with it
entries.text: Crossed the stepping stones with the compass in my fist and my thumb on the lever tail, no hopping. At the edge I flicked the tail out: the needle dropped, swung twice and settled in five breaths. West, straight out over the water, with the sun a hand to its left going in.
entries.title: It still knows west

entries.onMind: how many nights until the lines split
entries.text: Drew tonight's sunset line on the sheet next to last night's. I can't tell them apart; one night is too short to see it walk. Back home they never said where the sun goes. Nobody ever looked.
entries.title: Second line

entries.text: The stone ring I walked past cold an hour ago is burning now, with nobody at it. I stood at the brambles and watched it through the trunks the way I'd watch a joint I don't trust.
entries.title: Lit again

entries.text: Then something came back to it carrying something flat, and crouched. Small, low to the ground, black against the flames; too far and too dark to say more. I went to the stones the long way, wide of it. It's not my fire.
entries.title: Something low

entries.text: Lit the lantern on the east bank once I was across, then lifted the stone off the net bag and scooped out a double handful of meal. Still that dry edge at the back.
entries.title: A wet handful

entries.text: Ate the whole handful on the crate, a pinch at a time. Gritty, faintly bitter, and it sits in my stomach like ballast, which beats it sitting there empty. Trap tomorrow.
entries.title: Ate it anyway

entries.text: Lit only the bench lantern and turned the wick low; the other two stay dark to save oil. Started the trap: eight stalks bent around a ring of cord, lashed every hand-width.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.text: Outer cone done, a forearm long, wide end the size of my hat. Gaps between stalks under a finger, so a crayfish can't squeeze out the sides.
entries.title: Outer cone

entries.onMind: whether a lopsided door still keeps them in
entries.text: The inner cone's mouth won't hold. Every time I tie it to a thumb wide, the stalks spring and it opens back to three fingers. A ring of cord wrapped tight pulls it in, but now the door's lopsided. Good enough for a crayfish, probably. Not for me.
entries.title: Springy door

entries.text: Hammered the rounded lip of the compass step back up with the flat of the wrench, light taps, until it feels sharp under a fingernail. No hop test in the dark; I'll knock it off the bench and lose it in the leaves.
entries.title: Peened

entries.text: The owls again, both somewhere upstream over the water, the low one first and the high one after. Same order every night. My stomach answered too.
entries.title: The pair

entries.text: Pushed the inner cone into the outer one's mouth and lashed them at five points. On the fourth lash a stalk snapped and I had to splice in a new one. The door still sits lopsided, but it points the right way, in.
entries.title: Cone in a cone

entries.text: Tied the two crayfish heads from lunch on a cord through the middle, then lashed the back end shut. Anything that wants out has to find a lopsided thumb-wide hole facing the wrong way.
entries.title: Bait

entries.onMind: whether anything walks into it by morning
entries.text: Carried it to the east shallows by the bench lantern and sank it mouth downstream with a splash, a flat stone on top. Tied its cord to a root on the bank so the creek can't walk off with it.
entries.title: Night shift

entries.text: The fire past the water is still going, low and orange through the trunks. I turned the lantern down and didn't look for whoever keeps it.
entries.title: Still burning

entries.text: Twisted stalk fiber into cord on the crate, an arm's length at a time. The trap ate most of what I had. Three arm-lengths now, tight enough not to unlay.
entries.title: More cord

entries.text: Pried the flat stone off with the wrench and it rang on the rock. One crayfish inside, thumb-long, and while I watched a second one backed out the wide side of the lopsided door. Rebaited and sank it again.
entries.title: One aboard

entries.text: The fire past the water burns lower than it did an hour ago, and the air coming over smells of wet ash, like somebody threw water on it.
entries.title: Wet smoke

entries.text: Boiled it in the tin over the bench lantern and ate the tail. One bite. Cost more oil than it gave back, but the trap works, one way, mostly the right way.
entries.title: Supper, sort of

entries.text: Drew the trap on the sheet by lantern: a small cone two paces below the stepping stones on the east side. Only what I've walked goes on.
entries.title: On the sheet

entries.text: Pried the stone off and lifted it: two crayfish this time, one thumb-long and one smaller, and the bait heads picked down to shell. Carrying the whole trap home to fix the door while it's out.
entries.title: Two aboard

entries.text: The orange past the water sank to a red smudge and then I couldn't find it at all. Whoever keeps it put it to bed.
entries.title: Fire's down

entries.text: Boiled both in the tin over the bench lantern and ate them on the crate. Two tails is still not supper, and the oil can is lighter every night.
entries.title: Two bites

entries.text: Wrapped a second ring of cord around the door and bent each stalk end inward with the wrench jaws. Not round, but a thumb wide whichever way I measure it now.
entries.title: Rounder

entries.text: Sank the trap with its rounder door under the flat stone, tonight's three heads tied inside for bait, and knotted it to the root again.
entries.title: Back to work

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the meal was close to being food.
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and put a pinch of meal on my tongue. The dry edge at the back is smaller than at sundown, but it's there, so I spat it in the creek.
entries.title: Smaller edge

entries.reason: Three boils in one night made him count.
entries.text: Tipped the oil can toward the lantern and sloshed it. About a third of what my maker sent is left, and every crayfish I boil burns some of it.
entries.title: A third left

entries.text: The stone ring past the water cooks for somebody every night on wood, not oil. I keep thinking about those coals, and I don't like how much.
entries.title: Their coals

entries.text: Twisting cord, I heard the low one hoot its five over the tarp and the high one answer from upstream, late as usual.
entries.title: Pair again

entries.reason: He wanted to know if the second ring of cord kept them in.
entries.text: Lifted the stone by lantern: one crayfish, middling, and half the bait still there. Nothing got out past the rounder door.
entries.title: One more

entries.text: No orange past the water at all now. Whoever keeps that ring is asleep, and I should be too.
entries.title: Dark ring

entries.reason: Every boil costs oil, and one boil for many costs less.
entries.text: Dropped it in the dented tin with creek water instead of boiling it. One tail isn't worth the oil; by morning there'll be more, and I'll boil them all in one go.
entries.title: Saving it

entries.text: Marked the catches beside the trap on the sheet: one, two, one. Four in a night out of a cone of dead stalks.
entries.title: Tally
